name: Ulexite
toxicityNote: A borate mineral: do not ingest, avoid dust, wash hands after handling and do not make elixirs.
physical: Traditionally linked to eye strain relief by folk custom
Associated with relaxation for screen-weary people
Kept nearby by many for a calm, clear head
summary: Ulexite, nicknamed TV stone, carries light along fiber-like crystals to its surface, and crystal lore links it to insight, vision and clarity.
intro: Ulexite is the famous TV stone: a soft white borate mineral whose crystals grow as parallel fibers, much like fiber optic cables. When a flat, polished piece is placed over text or an image, the picture appears to float on the top surface of the stone, as though a tiny screen were embedded in it. The effect works because each fiber acts as a light pipe, carrying the image from the bottom to the top. Rough ulexite looks like cotton balls or white wool, and polished pieces look glassy and clear. It is a conversation starter on any shelf, and it makes people smile the first time they see it.
history: Ulexite was named after the German chemist Georg Ludwig Ulex, who first analyzed the mineral in the 1850s. It forms in dry lake beds, called playas, in desert regions where borate-rich waters evaporate, and the major deposits are in California, Nevada, Chile and Kazakhstan. Because it has long been mined as an ore of boron, it was known commercially before it became a collector favorite. The fibrous variety with its lens-like effect was nicknamed television stone in the twentieth century. There is no ancient folklore, so its metaphysical identity comes from its optical behavior and its association with sight.
meaning: The crystal community loves ulexite because it literally shows you what lies underneath. It is linked to the third eye and crown chakras, and practitioners use it as a metaphor and tool for insight: looking through the surface to see clearly. Many use it for scrying, meditation and visualization, and for situations where they want to see all sides of a problem. It is said to encourage open-mindedness and patience with slow-developing answers. Because of its fibrous structure, it also represents the idea that energy travels along invisible channels. Traditionally ulexite is associated with relaxed, clear thinking and a calm head, and is kept near work desks by those who spend long hours on screens.
howToUse: Set a polished ulexite on a page with a word or intention written on it and let the text appear on the top of the stone, a ritual often used to focus attention on a goal. Hold a piece while meditating, using its clarity as a focal point for the third eye. Keep it on your desk as a reminder to look at things from multiple angles, or place it on a nightstand with a journal for reflecting on dreams. A small stone fits in a palm for quiet moments between calls. Handle it gently, since it is soft.
care: Ulexite is soft and dissolves slowly in water, so keep it dry, and never soak or use it in elixirs. Cleanse with sound, smoke or a bed of selenite, and tolerate brief daylight though prolonged heat is best avoided. Dust it with a soft brush, and store it wrapped in cloth in a dry box, away from humidity and harder stones that could scratch the polished face. Wash your hands after handling it, particularly raw material.
identify: True ulexite shows a clear TV effect: text placed under the flat polished face appears on the top surface. Glass or acrylic look-alikes show the image only at the bottom, and optical calcite shows doubled images. Natural ulexite is very soft, scratches easily and has a silky, fibrous look when broken. The polished cut must follow the fiber direction for the effect to work, so slight variations are normal.

faq.q: Why is ulexite called TV stone?
faq.a: Ulexite grows as bundles of parallel fibers that carry light from one end to the other, like fiber optics. When polished flat, an image placed beneath appears on the top surface, like a miniature screen.
Crystal lovers use ulexite for insight, scrying and clear perspective. It is a favorite for meditation, vision work and as a desk stone to encourage seeing situations from different angles.
